sense.text:
“Now therefore, my sons, be ye zealous for the law, and give your lives for the covenant of your fathers.” The feast of dedication is the warriors' feast. Zeal for the law includes giving one's life for the covenant of the fathers. A man who will not make that commitment needs to get the hell out the way of the brothers prepared to do the work. This is a call to fight for the laws and the nation, not merely to attend a celebration.

The brothers doing thirty, sixty, one hundred or three hundred sixty-five days of camp are examples of that labour. The number of days is not the point; going out and giving the people the word of God is. The wisdom, knowledge and understanding bestowed upon Israel must be used to reach the earth.

The repeated presence in Springfield after Sonya Massey's killing shows what giving one's life to the covenant looks like. The brothers came in numbers over multiple weeks, met the family and gave the community hope through their unity. Meeting a family member again on Beale Street showed that people remembered that support. The same obligation is applied to standing with Kendrick Johnson's family: our people's children are our own, and their suffering must not be forgotten.

Fight for the men, women and children of the nation. When the people call, show up with answers and with the understanding of God and Christ. The feast remembers taking back the temple from those who profaned it and rededicating it to the Most High. The present work must carry that same commitment rather than leave the people looking for help that never comes.

precepts.why:
“For what if some did not believe? shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect?” Unbelief does not stop God's truth or cancel Israel's identity. “God forbid: yea, let God be true, but every man a liar;” Let God establish the matter rather than treating the objections of apologists as authority above the Bible.

The identity of the people is connected to the prophecies of slave ships, service to enemies, changed names and nationalities, and the lost sheep. Those occupying Israel today are challenged to show how those conditions fit their own history. The argument is not surrendered because someone refuses to believe it.

The opposition online is presented as a response to the work already being done. Brothers must not become discouraged or imagine that hostile videos mean the truth has been defeated. Continue going out with the commandments and the covenant; another man's unbelief cannot make the faith of God without effect.

sense.text:
“Then began the fear of Judas and his brethren, and an exceeding great dread, to fall upon the nations round about them:” Judas and his brethren brought fear upon the nations around them. The present unity and public work of Israel are connected to that same fear: the nations see men moving together in the spirit of God and keeping the commandments. Their efforts to fight back do not mean that Israel should stop.

The victory comes from God. Prayer acknowledges that the people are not winning by their own power. The work of reaching the earth with the scriptures continues because the Most High supplies the strength, even when opposition comes from many directions.

precepts.why:
“And after three days and an half the Spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet; and great fear fell upon them which saw them.” The three days and a half are understood as three hundred fifty years. The spirit of life entering the people is the commandments of God coming into Israel, bringing the people to their feet. Their renewed obedience and visible work produce fear in those who see them.

This is not treated as merely Christ's presence among believers during the Roman captivity, as though the whole event had already been exhausted then. The standing up and the fear are applied to Israel awakening now. As in the account of Judas, the enemies' dread follows the power of God working through his people, not an advantage in numbers.

sense.text:
“Unto whom Judas answered, It is no hard matter for many to be shut up in the hands of a few; and with the God of heaven it is all one, to deliver with a great multitude, or a small company:” A few can overcome many when the God of heaven gives deliverance. The strength of the work is not a head count. Israel can face the world's opposition because God supplies the power.

The questions about how so many men can gather, march in step, know the scriptures and maintain order have an answer: the commandments of God. That discipline is not difficult for God to produce among a people who obey him. Those rejecting the commandments cannot explain that spirit while claiming the same connection to Christ.

Hostile comments, restrictions on visibility online and efforts to stop the message are reasons to keep moving, not proof that the people have no power. Others would not fight the work so hard if nothing were happening. Continue reaching the streets and standing with the nation even when the opposition has resources beyond those of the brothers.

“Again, he sent forth other servants,” The repeated sending is applied to continually coming out into the streets and highways. Service to the people cannot be a single appearance followed by disappearance. The brothers returning in unity to support their community show that continuing obligation in practice.

“Thou sittest and speakest against thy brother; thou slanderest thine own mother’s son.” Speaking against one's brother and slandering one's own mother's son are applied to the apologists attacking Israel. The same hostility is also attributed to Esau. Opposition to the people does not become righteous simply because it is delivered as religious criticism.

“These things hast thou done, and I kept silence; thou thoughtest that I was altogether such an one as thyself:” God's silence is mistaken for agreement, and men make him an image of themselves. The white image of Christ is an example: those promoting it should prove that Christ is white rather than continually demanding that Israel defend the opposite.

The image identified as Caesar Borgia appears on taxis, signs and posters in Haiti and Ghana, even in a Kentucky Fried Chicken restaurant in Ghana. Its widespread use is contrasted with the claim that nobody is trying to make Christ white. A picture promoted continually across countries and institutions shapes the people's understanding of God. Its acceptance must not be confused with proof.

“For it is better for us to die in battle, than to behold the calamities of our people and our sanctuary.” It is better to die fighting than to stand by while the nation and sanctuary suffer calamity. The feast of dedication honours that resolve. Living in shame while the people are destroyed is not the standard for men of God.

The challenge is brought home to men who want the position of leaders without discipline, responsibility or self-control. A woman's criticism of men who demand submission while lacking order in their own lives introduces the need to examine that weakness. The warrior's commitment has to shape conduct, not remain a slogan.

“Whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust.” The promises belong to Israel. The divine nature is not the world's nature; the commandments show the difference. Escape from corruption requires leaving the lust that drives the surrounding society.

Corruption is applied to sexual disorder, including men lying with men, women lying with women, paedophilia and abortion, and to a man so controlled by lust that he will pursue sex without restraint. A man cannot excuse the inability to govern his own body while expecting a woman to recognize his leadership. God's promises call the people out of those patterns.

The same separation includes honouring God's feast days rather than choosing the world's holidays. The feast of dedication is about the recovery and cleansing of the temple, not continuing the habits of the people who profaned it.

“And beside this, giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge;” Faith must be developed with diligence, virtue and knowledge. Virtue concerns the strength and character needed to govern oneself. The work of becoming a man of God includes learning and applying the scriptures, not merely professing belief.

“And to knowledge temperance; and to temperance patience; and to patience godliness;” Temperance is self-control. A man needs command of his appetites, patience and godliness rather than continually giving in to sexual desire or other impulses. These qualities are built together; the discipline expected of a warrior is also required in his private conduct.

“And to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity.” Godliness must produce brotherly kindness and charity. Charity includes bearing one another's burdens and caring for the body, rather than treating spiritual growth as a private title or an excuse to ignore the needs of the nation. The men should become more temperate, patient and godly while continuing the work together.

precepts.why: “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia,” Peter writes to the scattered strangers in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia. These are Israelites scattered among those places. The audience must be identified before the promises are applied. Galatia is also the region addressed in Paul's letter to the Galatians; a foreign place name does not by itself make the people another nation.

“But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:” The chosen generation, royal priesthood, holy nation and peculiar people are Israel. This identifies the people meant by the promises and the call out of darkness. The national description is not discarded because the letter is in the New Testament or because the people live scattered among other nations.

“Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises;” Adoption, glory, covenants, the giving of the law, service and promises belong to the Israelites. The glory is connected to the kingdom. The list establishes who received the promises Peter describes and why the scattered people are being called back to God's nature.

Scripture is joined to scripture to establish the audience. The claim that the promises have no particular national recipient is challenged by the explicit naming of Israel and by the covenant and law entrusted to that people.

sense.text:
“Cursed shall be thy basket and thy store.” The curse on basket and store is applied to the people's economic condition and lack of ownership. The businesses supplying the neighbourhood are owned by others while Israel remains dependent. That condition follows breaking the commandments.

The Bible is the manual for changing the people, including how men govern themselves and how the nation works together. Unity and obedience could build the people's own businesses and resources instead of leaving them permanently dependent on outsiders. Demanding authority without discipline or the ability to provide does not repair the condition.

“Therefore shalt thou serve thine enemies which the Lord shall send against thee, in hunger, and in thirst, and in nakedness, and in want of all things: and he shall put a yoke of iron upon thy neck, until he have destroyed thee.” Israel's enemies are real nations, not merely other black people. The condition is applied to blacks, Hispanics and Native American Indians: hunger, thirst, nakedness, want of all things and the iron yoke describe the captivity and dependence of the people. The Lord sent those enemies against Israel because of disobedience.

The dependence reaches the necessities of life. Food, water and clothing are controlled by others. Memphis's water supply illustrates that even a resource beneath the people's own city is not in their hands to govern as they please. Birth, death and marriage certificates likewise show how life is conducted under the authority of the nations. Declaring that one needs none of those arrangements does not remove the captivity.

The iron yoke is connected to what literally happened to the people. Claiming faith while refusing to face that history, or spending one's effort fighting brothers who are doing the work, leaves the underlying condition untouched. The responsibility is to show the works that accompany the faith and help the nation.

precepts.why:
“Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith,” Saying that one has faith is not the same as showing it in action. The challenge is directed to men claiming the truth while contributing nothing to the work and continually criticizing those who go out.

An impressive online name about destroying the Gentiles proves nothing without visible labour. A critic who says the sisters should be addressed differently is challenged to demonstrate that work himself. The willingness to learn from a better example is present, but an accusation without an example is not a substitute for serving the people. Put the claimed faith to work instead of leaving the nation in its existing condition.

sense.text:
“We lie down in our shame, and our confusion covereth us: for we have sinned” Shame is applied to remaining content in service to the enemies and making no effort to change the people's condition. Men who will not work online or in the streets, will not govern their desires and will not take responsibility for their families continue lying down in that shame. Knowing the name Israel while refusing the work of repentance does not remove it.

The congregation must be able to confront real problems honestly. Confusion in sexual conduct cannot be hidden under claims of knowledge or leadership. Men and women need correction, self-control and the application of the commandments rather than permission to continue whatever they desire.

Confusion is also seen in choosing Thanksgiving over the feast of dedication and Easter over Passover. The people hear the scriptures but defend customs that are not there. Sin explains the shame; the way out is not to keep serving and then argue against those calling for change.

precepts.why: “Therefore shalt thou serve thine enemies which the Lord shall send against thee,” Service to the enemies explains the shame. The Lord brought those enemies upon the people, yet many have become comfortable serving and refuse to work for a change in the nation's condition. The verse is brought back repeatedly to make that connection concrete.

“And the Lord God said, It is not good that the man should be alone;” Men and women need one another. The claim that a man can do without women is rejected alongside the message telling black women they need no man. Hatred of one's own women is not a foundation for marriage or for restoring the nation.

The question about living on an island without the opposite sex exposes the failure to think about the people's future. Men and women together can continue the people; a society refusing that relationship cannot. A man professing Christianity should not need to deliberate over whether the absence of all women would be good. God's judgment that the man should not be alone is already given.

sense.text:
“Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.” To spoil the people is to pervert and destroy them. Greek and Roman philosophies in the earlier setting are connected to the American philosophies and customs promoted now. Paul's warning is against traditions of men and the world's rudiments, not against God's commandments.

The feast of tabernacles, day of atonement, feast of dedication and new moon are contrasted with Thanksgiving and other man-made holidays. People reject the days God gives them while slaughtering turkeys by the billions for a single day that has nothing to do with Christ. Saying that there is nothing wrong with thankfulness does not answer whom the observance honours or where God commanded it.

Do not use Paul to defend idolatry and man-made religion. A passage warning against human traditions cannot honestly be used to replace God's days with those same traditions.

precepts.why:
“O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:” Guard what has been committed to the people rather than accepting profane and vain babblings or falsely named science. The warning is joined to the philosophers and religious customs used to draw Israel away from the days God established.

The regard for Esau as a god because of planes, technology and other achievements is challenged. That impression was encountered while teaching in Africa. Technological possession does not explain where the wisdom and knowledge came from, and it is no reason to surrender the commandments or accept the religion of the people holding those resources.

sense.text:
“Judah mourneth, and the gates thereof languish; they are black unto the ground;” The objection that blackness refers only to a condition is challenged by the physical descriptions in Lamentations. The same prophet's language about face and skin is brought alongside the description of Judah. The black identity of the people is not surrendered to an explanation that removes those words from consideration.

Leaving the congregation over this point is also connected to the need for honesty about one's conduct. A man who has not been doing the street work should not present reluctance to teach as though an active ministry had been halted solely by this question. The interpretation must be considered with the scriptures actually describing the people.

precepts.why:
“Their visage is blacker than a coal;” Visage means a person's face. The comparison is therefore applied to the face itself, and coal is brought forward as the visible comparison. The wording is used to challenge the claim that blackness cannot describe the people's physical appearance. Jeremiah is identified as the same prophet speaking in both books.

The discussion also contrasts the feast of dedication with Thanksgiving. Dedication remembers overcoming the enemies, recovering the temple, cleansing it and rededicating it to the Most High: independence and freedom. Thanksgiving is connected to conquest, the taking of the people's resources and the sale of slaves, rather than to Israel's own deliverance.

“Our skin was black like an oven because of the terrible famine.” The word is skin, and the comparison is to an oven. The oven in the ancient setting is understood as black, not a modern white appliance. The attempt to make famine mean that otherwise white skin became black is rejected. Face, coal, skin and oven are joined to establish the physical description being defended.

sense.text:
“And had a wall great and high, and had twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names written thereon, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel:” There are twelve gates, with the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel written upon them. The claim that there are only two gates is challenged by the stated number and the tribal names. The question of which gate a person will enter directs attention to Israel's identity. The angels guarding the gates are described as black.

The purpose is to give black men, black women and the people a positive understanding of who they are, removing the confusion imposed by white supremacy Christianity. Those still caught in it are not treated as people who can never learn: we once needed the same instruction, and wisdom freely received must be freely given.

Christ died for the nation of Israel. The law connected to his death is the sacrificial system, not permission to abandon every commandment. The distinction includes ceremonial laws governing holy days and civil laws governing conduct toward one another. Leaving a woman to bear and raise a child alone is an example of the uncivil behaviour the people must change.

“But they said, We will not come forth, neither will we do the king’s commandment, to profane the sabbath day.” Refusal to profane the Sabbath is the example of refusing conformity. Do not betray the laws of God for something desired from this nation. The warrior's feast calls for continuing faithfulness rather than lying down in shame or accepting the king's commands above God's.

Keep applying pressure through the work, becoming more temperate, patient and godly. The unity of men who know and can explain the scriptures is contrasted with a gathering that can only shout Jesus without supplying doctrine. Knowledge of the word must direct the people and their conduct.

precepts.why:
“But one of them that spake first said thus, What wouldest thou ask or learn of us? we are ready to die, rather than to transgress the laws of our fathers.” Choose death over defilement. The resolve to die rather than transgress the fathers' laws explains the refusal to obey the king in profaning the Sabbath. This is the mind commemorated in the feast of dedication.

The claim that Christ removed the obligation to keep the commandments is challenged by that commitment. Salvation concerns deliverance for the people who are oppressed and who received the law and covenant. The oppressor possessing the weapons is distinguished from the people needing deliverance. Israel must not trade the commandments for the religion or approval of the nations ruling over them.

sense.text:
“Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days:” Meat and drink concern the meat offerings, drink offerings and burnt offerings associated with the holy days. The warning is against demanding those sacrifices from people keeping the new moon, Passover, day of atonement or Sabbath after Christ's offering. It is not an instruction to stop observing the days themselves.

The objection that observing a day requires producing its former animal offering confuses the day with the sacrifice attached to it. Christ supplies the answer to the offering. The people should not let someone use that objection to turn them from God's calendar or tell them not to fast on the day of atonement.

Christ's presence at the feast of dedication and the apostles' work in Solomon's porch show the example being followed. The demand for a biblical command to keep Christmas, decorate a tree, put presents beneath it or leave milk and cookies for Santa Claus exposes the contrast: those are traditions of men, while the scriptures show Christ keeping dedication. Do not let the world's customs change the mind about God's days.

“Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.” A shadow passes away when what it points toward arrives. The sacrifices were the shadow of Christ's offering. The former bodies were bulls and goats; now the body is Christ's.

The final words about the body must not be omitted when the passage is used to argue that the feast days have disappeared. Christ replaces the sacrifices tied to those commandments. His body is the substance to which the former offerings pointed, and that distinction allows the people to understand why obedience and the holy days continue.

precepts.why:
“Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.” The earlier warning in the chapter identifies the danger as philosophy, vain deceit, human tradition and the world's rudiments. The new moon and Sabbath were given by God; they are not inventions of men. Treating them as the very traditions Paul condemns reverses his warning.

Follow Christ's example. His observance of dedication makes the contrast concrete, while the replacement of God's days with man-made holidays follows the tradition against which Paul warns.

sense.text: “And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter.” Christ was in Jerusalem at the feast of dedication in winter. Dedication remembers defeating the Greeks, cleansing the profaned temple and rededicating it to the Most High. Christ's presence is proof that he kept the high holy days.

“And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon’s porch.” Solomon's porch was a public place at the temple where people gathered to discuss the word of God and where miracles occurred. Christ taught there, and the apostles later worked in the same setting. The temple was open and people assembled around the scriptures.

Some Jews asked Christ to tell them plainly whether he was the Christ. He had already told them, and the works done in his Father's name bore witness of him. Their doubt is not evidence that every Israelite rejected him. The passage concerns the people addressing him at that moment.

“But ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep, as I said unto you. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me:” These unbelieving Jews were not his sheep. The sheep hear his voice, are known by him and follow him. Being part of Israel does not mean that every individual responds faithfully; the distinction is made within the people rather than by claiming that none of them believed.

Certain Jews took up stones after Christ spoke of his unity with the Father. When he asked which good work deserved stoning, they answered that their accusation was blasphemy because a man made himself God. The group attempting to stone him must not be substituted for the whole nation.

“Jesus answered them, Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods?” Christ answered from the law. Those to whom God's word came were called gods, and the scripture could not be broken. He used that written authority to answer the charge against the one whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world.

Following Christ means returning to the scriptures when challenged, rather than placing man's argument over God's word. His answer about being the Son of God comes from what is already written. Let God be true instead of accepting a claim simply because religious opponents repeat it.

“And many resorted unto him, and said, John did no miracle: but all things that John spake of this man were true. And many believed on him there.” Many came to Christ and acknowledged that what John had said about him was true, although John did no miracle. Many believed there. This explicitly defeats the assertion that all the Jews rejected Christ. Some did not believe, but others heard his voice and followed him; the unbelief of the former did not cancel God's truth.

precepts.why: “And by the hands of the apostles were many signs and wonders wrought among the people; (and they were all with one accord in Solomon’s porch.” The apostles worked signs and wonders among the people and gathered with one accord in Solomon's porch. This identifies the same temple setting in which Christ walked. The porch was a place of public teaching, miracles and unity around the word of God.

“And as the lame man which was healed held Peter and John, all the people ran together unto them in the porch that is called Solomon’s, greatly wondering.” The healed lame man held Peter and John while the people ran together to Solomon's porch in wonder. People were there to witness the healing and hear the scriptures. The scene helps explain why Christ could be surrounded and questioned in that same public place during dedication.

sense.text: “Jesus answered and said unto them, Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” The temple Christ speaks of is his body. Its destruction and raising in three days concern his death and resurrection. Christ is Israel's last temple because the coming sacrifice was fulfilled in him rather than remaining in the former offerings.

The Jews answered about the building that had taken forty-six years to construct, asking how he would raise it in three days. “But he spake of the temple of his body.” The distinction resolves the statement: he was speaking of his body, not promising a three-day reconstruction of the physical structure.

The former sacrifices were a shadow pointing forward to Christ. A shadow is temporary; his body is what those offerings anticipated. Understanding that connection prevents the change in sacrifices from being turned into an abolition of God's commandments.

precepts.why:
“Yet it pleased the Lord to bruise him; he hath put him to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin,” The one bruised is Christ. His soul becomes the offering for sin. That was foretold before his death and explains how the temple of his body replaces the sacrifices that pointed toward him.

The offering is not an accidental interruption of God's plan. The Lord appointed Christ's suffering, and the body raised after death is the reality behind the earlier sacrificial shadow.

sense.text:
“To whom coming, as unto a living stone, disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God, and precious,” Christ is the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious to God. His death was necessary for what followed. The rejection was by scribes, Pharisees and certain Jews who followed them, not by every person in Israel. That distinction agrees with the many who believed in him in John.

The audience has already been identified as the scattered Israelites, the chosen generation and royal priesthood. Their connection to Christ does not require abandoning that identity.

“Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ.” The people become lively stones as the old man dies and they become new creatures living in Christ's faith. Together they form a spiritual house with Christ as the foundation and chief cornerstone.

The people are the holy priesthood, and Christ is the chief high priest. A man in an Israelite camp cannot take that position for himself. A sinful human priest would first need an offering for his own sins; Christ's role is not a title for a man to claim while the same problems remain in his own life.

The spiritual sacrifices are obedience and praise, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. This is why the people continue keeping the feast days. The sacrifice has changed through Christ, but worship and obedience have not become unnecessary.

“And it shall come to pass, that from one new moon to another, and from one sabbath to another, shall all flesh come to worship before me, saith the Lord.” This is future prophecy: worship from one new moon to another and one Sabbath to another will come to pass. Christ could not have abolished those observances in the sense claimed while God still requires them in the coming kingdom.

All flesh includes the nations. Those who now fight the new moon and Sabbath will have to keep them too. Wanting the kingdom while resisting its commandments and God's people is contradictory. The coming order must be accepted on God's terms rather than remade according to the world's traditions.

The woman of Canaan called upon the Son of David for mercy because her daughter was grievously vexed with a devil. Christ initially answered nothing, and the disciples asked that she be sent away because she cried after them. “But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” The explicit mission to the lost sheep of Israel is brought against the claim that the account promises the same salvation indiscriminately to every nation.

“Then came she and worshipped him, saying, Lord, help me.” The woman came humbly for help. That attitude is contrasted with nations cursing Israel, disputing the people's identity and continuing to promote a white image of Christ. If they want a blessing, they should bless God's people rather than attack them. Her request acknowledges where the help is found.

“But he answered and said, It is not meet to take the children’s bread, and to cast it to dogs.” The children and the dogs are distinguished. The children's bread belongs to Israel. Christ's words are used to establish the place of God's sons and daughters rather than the denial and insults directed at them by those claiming a share in their kingdom.

“And she said, Truth, Lord: yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table.” The woman acknowledged the master and accepted the crumbs. Her humility is contrasted with those who refuse to acknowledge Israel as God's children or accept service in the kingdom. She was prepared to take the portion available to her instead of claiming the children's bread.

The crumbs are connected to the gleanings left after the harvest. The harvest and bread belong to Israel, while provision is left for the stranger. The distinction gives the woman help without making her the owner of what belongs to the children. The nations' participation is understood as cleaving to Israel in service, not taking Israel's place.

precepts.why:
“And the people shall take them, and bring them to their place: and the house of Israel shall possess them in the land of the Lord for servants and handmaids:” The house of Israel possesses the nations as servants and handmaids in the Lord's land. This is joined to the woman's acceptance of the crumbs and of the master's place. The kingdom, like the harvest, belongs to Israel; the strangers receive provision while serving.

The nations' reluctance to surrender their present kingdom is contrasted with the humility of the Canaanite woman. Black Christians are challenged for defending white supremacy Christianity and the present order instead of seeking God's kingdom. Israel must also stop lying down in shame and train its men to govern themselves, work and take responsibility.

The appeal to bless Israel is repeated: cursing the people will not obtain the blessing being sought. Those wishing to cleave to Israel must accept the place described rather than continue fighting the identity and laws of the children of God.

sense.text:
“And when ye reap the harvest of your land, thou shalt not make clean riddance of the corners of thy field when thou reapest, neither shalt thou gather any gleaning of thy harvest: thou shalt leave them unto the poor, and to the stranger:” When God blesses Israel in the land and the people reap their harvest, they must not take every last piece. The corners and fallen gleanings are left for the poor and the stranger. God's law provides for those who do not own the harvest.

This explains the crumbs from the master's table. The bread is the harvest belonging to the children; the gleanings are provision for the strangers who acknowledge that order. Israel's blessing is not permission to strip away every resource from everyone else. The law leaves something for those receiving help, as the Canaanite woman was ready to receive the crumbs.

precepts.why:
“If thieves came to thee, if robbers by night, (how art thou cut off!) would they not have stolen till they had enough? if the grapegatherers came to thee, would they not leave some grapes? How are the things of Esau searched out! how are his hidden things sought up!” Thieves normally stop when they have enough, and grape gatherers leave some grapes. Esau is contrasted with those limits: Esau takes everything. The impoverishment of countries is connected to that complete taking of resources.

The question about Esau's hidden things is applied to the policies, plans and declarations by which that power operates. How those things are searched out and how the taking is stopped are set against the law requiring Israel to leave gleanings. The difference is between God's provision for the poor and stranger and an order that removes everything. Esau is called the damn devil in that contrast.

sense.text:
“Blessed are they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city.” Doing the commandments gives right to the tree of life, understood as eternal life, and entrance through the city's gates. The commandments have not been done away with. Christ's offering concerns the sacrifices tied to them, not permission to abandon obedience.

There are twelve gates, returning to the names of Israel's tribes. The feast days and the new month belong to the people and point toward the Lord and his coming. Continue the work with confidence rather than become discouraged by opponents with larger audiences. Their response to the work shows that the message is being heard.

“For without are dogs,” The dogs outside are connected to the distinction in the Canaanite woman's answer. The nations are called to humility toward Israel and to cleave as servants and handmaids, rather than claiming the children's kingdom while cursing the children. The closing appeal is to bless God's people and accept the order already described.
